title: Hakimoglu v. Trump Taj Mahal Associates
lead: A gambler’s tort effort to recover past losses remained dismissed, while his intoxication defense to the casino’s separate $700,000 credit claim survived for factual development.

actors.name: Hakimoglu
actors.role: Gambler asserting affirmative dram-shop claims and defending unpaid markers

actors.name: Trump Taj Mahal Associates and related defendants
actors.role: Casino parties defending the claims; Taj Mahal counterclaimed on credit

actors.name: Judge Simandle
actors.role: District judge deciding reconsideration, partial summary judgment, and certification

proceedings: Earlier tort dismissal reconsidered after an intervening jurisdiction decision; reconsideration denied, casino’s partial-summary-judgment motion denied without prejudice, and affirmative-claim dismissal certified under Rule 54(b) for immediate appeal.
limits: This December 23, 1994 district-court stage is not an appellate remand or incapacity finding. The assigned note includes material not located in this cited opinion. Original date inconsistencies in the estoppel account do not establish an additional transaction.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Hakimoglu alleged that free alcohol accompanied repeated gambling losses
sections.cue: Introduce the allegations and the separate debt claim.
paragraphs: Hakimoglu alleged that Taj Mahal defendants enticed him to gamble repeatedly in 1992 and 1993, supplied free alcohol in his hotel room, and continually served complimentary four-to-five-ounce gin martinis while he gambled. He said they kept serving after he became visibly and substantially intoxicated, allowed more gambling, and extended additional markers, causing losses exceeding $2 million. These allegations were accepted for dismissal analysis, not found true.

Although the complaint named negligence, intentional and malicious conduct, and unjust enrichment, Hakimoglu consolidated the theories into a common-law dram-shop claim. He did not present a general negligence claim, an affirmative contract claim, or an implied private remedy under casino regulations.

Trump Taj Mahal Associates separately counterclaimed for $700,000 advanced through five counterchecks during April 25, 1993 gambling. Deposited May 12, they came back unpaid May 20 marked “account closed.” The casino also sought $17,750 in baccarat commissions, or vigorish, but excluded that amount from its partial-summary-judgment motion. Hakimoglu defended the credit obligation on intoxication-based incapacity, distinct from an affirmative tort right to recover money already lost.

sections.title: An intervening appellate decision prompted reconsideration, not automatic revival
sections.cue: Separate judicial authority to hear a dispute from a valid cause of action.
paragraphs: On March 31, 1994, Judge Simandle had found subject-matter jurisdiction but predicted New Jersey would not recognize the proposed dram-shop claim for gambling losses. The Third Circuit’s September 6 decision in Greate Bay Hotel & Casino v. Tose then held that the Casino Control Commission lacked exclusive primary jurisdiction over such disputes. A note called a common-law duty to prevent known-intoxicated gambling reasonably arguable but expressly left its existence undecided.

Simandle invited further briefing and argument. Reconsideration required more than disagreement or repetition; intervening persuasive authority or new facts could matter. But Greate Bay decided jurisdiction, not substantive liability. Rule 12(b)(1)’s jurisdictional question differed from Rule 12(b)(6)’s sufficiency inquiry. The appellate observation warranted examination without requiring a new tort remedy.

sections.title: The court declined to extend dram-shop law to these financial losses
sections.cue: Explain the prediction of state law and its limits.
paragraphs: Sitting in diversity, the court had to predict New Jersey law. Miller v. Zoby had rejected an implied damages remedy for casino-credit regulation violations without legislative intent. Other federal predictions were more favorable to gamblers, but Simandle distinguished them and considered contrary reservations and later developments. He did not treat extensive casino regulation as automatically displacing every common-law action.

New Jersey dram-shop cases protected people injured by negligent alcohol service, including patrons, while comparative-fault decisions also emphasized voluntary consumption. The court found no state authority extending the doctrine to gambling losses. Those losses differed from traffic injuries, falls, and fights, and neither the legislature nor state supreme court had supplied the requested expansion.

The court reasoned that the patron initially chose gambling, baccarat depended on chance rather than necessarily impaired skill, and causation was difficult because sober patrons could lose and intoxicated ones win. Years-later claims lacked the objective accident and contemporaneous alcohol measurements common in injury cases; surveillance could be recycled after thirty days without a reported incident. Regulation deterred misconduct, and ordinary incapacity defenses limited collection of credit. The court noted regulatory silence about compulsory refunds without judging that policy’s wisdom. These were reasons against predicting liability, not findings that alcohol never affects gambling behavior.

Reconsideration was denied, leaving the affirmative claims dismissed. Ordinary contract defenses such as incapacity, duress, and unconscionability nevertheless remained available against the casino’s signed credit obligations. The court’s doubts about mutuality in individual regulated games did not erase that distinction.

sections.title: The casino’s estoppel argument depended on disputed knowledge and reliance
sections.cue: Explain why the credit defense survived without being proved.
paragraphs: Taj Mahal argued that equitable estoppel barred incapacity because Hakimoglu had consulted counsel and threatened alcohol-related gambling litigation against Caesars shortly before returning to Taj Mahal. Simandle recognized the possible unfairness of someone knowingly using that theory to keep winnings but contest losses. Estoppel could apply in contract and was not merely the tort doctrine of assumption of risk. Yet it required justified, reasonable detrimental reliance by an innocent party, not simply substantial reliance.

The casino supplied a letter and deposition excerpts but no affidavits or certifications establishing its knowledge of Hakimoglu’s drinking and gambling problems, or sufficient details of his marker and countercheck practices. Hakimoglu testified that he warned his casino host about excessive service and intoxication, but the single submitted deposition page did not identify when. Its relevance therefore remained uncertain. The surrounding circumstances and the casino’s knowledge presented genuine issues, without establishing either that the warning occurred at a relevant time or that estoppel could never succeed.

The casino alternatively said gambling enjoyment could not be returned. The court answered that the relevant credit consideration was $700,000 in chips. Because his checks bounced, Hakimoglu retained his own $700,000. If incapacity failed, Taj Mahal could recover that sum; if it succeeded, the casino could recover neither the money nor compensation for consumed atmosphere. That conditional explanation awarded nothing. Partial summary judgment was denied without prejudice.

sections.title: The court certified the dismissed claims while the counterclaim continued
sections.cue: End with the different intoxication standards and exact orders.
paragraphs: The dismissal resolved all affirmative claims, while the credit counterclaim remained. Under Rule 54(b), the court found no just reason to delay final judgment on the separate claims. The tort theories concerned losses on many occasions; the counterclaim involved one credit transaction. Their intoxication thresholds also differed. Visible, obvious intoxication under the proposed tort theory did not alone prove contractual incapacity. Citing Seminara, a state capacity decision, the court required intoxication so excessive and complete that the person could not appreciate the act’s nature and consequences.

On December 23, 1994, Simandle denied reconsideration, denied the casino’s partial-summary-judgment motion without prejudice, and certified the affirmative-claim dismissal for appeal. Novel recurring state-law questions and lack of cognizable prejudice supported certification. Counterclaim litigation and possible renewed summary judgment could continue; trial timing and any brief stay pending appeal were reserved. No remand, completed trial, incapacity finding, or $700,000 recovery occurred in this opinion.
